kinds.d: Barium sulfate mineral specimen: bladed and tabular crystals, rosettes and clusters, often blue, golden or colourless.

x.d: Radiating baryte nodules found near Bologna in the 17th century by Vincenzo Casciarolo; phosphorescent after calcining.
Barite from Alston Moor, Frizington and Cleator Moor, Cumbria, England.
Salmon-coloured barite with cerussite from Morocco.
Barite from Baia Sprie and Cavnic, Romania.
Immense barite crystals from the Elandsrand gold mine, Carletonville, South Africa.
Barite from the Creede district, the Book Cliffs and Elk Creek, South Dakota.

kinds.d: Strontium sulfate mineral specimen: pale blue crystals and geode linings.

x.d: Pale blue celestine crystals and geodes from Sakoany near Mahajanga, Madagascar.
x.dt: blue crystals in geodes · thumbnail to cabinet

x.d: Celestine from Crystal Cave, South Bass Island, Ohio, home of the largest known celestine geode, 11 m wide.
Celestine from Girgenti and elsewhere in Sicily, with sulfur.
White and orange celestine from Yate near Bristol, extracted commercially until April 1991.
Celestine from the Scofield quarry, Maybee, Michigan.

kinds.d: Calcium sulfate dihydrate mineral specimen: selenite blades, satin spar, desert roses and cave crystals.

x.d: Transparent bladed gypsum crystals, the largest crystals in nature, up to 12 m.
Giant gypsum crystals up to 11 m from the Naica mine caves, Chihuahua, found in April 2000.

v.d: largest crystal 11.4 m long, about 12 tonnes

x.d: Silky fibrous form of gypsum.
Very fine-grained white or lightly tinted gypsum used for ornament.
Opaque flower-like gypsum clusters containing sand, formed in arid areas.
Curved gypsum specimens from Santa Eulalia, Chihuahua.
Gypsum speleothems from Lechuguilla Cave, New Mexico.

kinds.d: Calcium sulfate mineral specimen: blue-grey crystals, massive pieces and carved angelite.

x.d: Semi-transparent blue-grey anhydrite from Peru, a trade name used for tumbled stones and carvings.
Anhydrite from Naica, Chihuahua, Mexico.
Gemmy anhydrite crystals from the Simplon Tunnel, Valais, Switzerland.
Scaly granular anhydrite from Volpino, near Bergamo, Lombardy, cut as an ornamental stone.
Anhydrite from Hall, Tirol, where it was first found in 1794; named by Werner in 1804.

kinds.d: Lead sulfate mineral specimen: glassy, adamantine crystals from lead deposits, often on galena.

x.d: Transparent colourless anglesite crystals with many faces from Monteponi, Sardinia.
Very large anglesite crystals from Tsumeb and the Kombat mine, Namibia.
Fine anglesite crystals from the Touissit mine, near Oujda, Morocco.
Small brownish-yellow crystals from Parys Mountain, Anglesey, type locality first recognised by Withering in 1783.
Large anglesite crystals from Broken Hill, New South Wales, and Dundas, Tasmania.

kinds.d: Copper sulfate hydroxide mineral specimen: emerald-green needle crystals and druses.

x.d: Large brochantite crystals from Bisbee, Arizona.
Brochantite from Nizhny Tagil and Gumeshevsk, Urals, the early source.
Brochantite from Chuquicamata and Collahuasi and other Chilean copper mines.
Brochantite from Serifos, Greece.
Brochantite pseudomorphous after malachite, azurite or chrysocolla.

kinds.d: Lead copper sulfate hydroxide mineral specimen: deep azure-blue crystals, usually small.

x.d: Fine linarite crystals from Red Gill and other mines of the Caldbeck Fells, Cumbria.
x.dt: crystals on galena · thumbnail to miniature

x.d: Linarite from the Blanchard mine, Hansonburg district, New Mexico.
Large linarite crystals from Tsumeb, Namibia.
Type-locality linarite from Linares, Jaén, Spain, first identified in 1822.
Large crystals from the Kisamori mine, Akita Prefecture, Japan.
Linarite from Darwin, Inyo County, California.

kinds.d: Copper aluminium sulfate hydroxide mineral specimen: sky-blue velvety needles and sprays.

x.d: Exceptional cyanotrichite from the Grandview (Last Chance) mine, Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona.
Cyanotrichite from the Cap Garonne mine, Var, France.
Type-locality cyanotrichite from Moldova Nouă, Banat, Romania, first described in 1839.
Large sprays from the Mex-Tex mine, Hansonburg district, New Mexico.

kinds.d: Lead molybdate mineral specimen: thin red, orange and yellow tabular crystals, prized for colour.

x.d: Deep red, well-formed wulfenite crystals from the Red Cloud mine, La Paz County, Arizona (state mineral since 2017).

v.n: Red Cloud mine, Silver district, La Paz Co.

x.dt: red tablets on matrix · miniature to cabinet

x.d: Very thick tabular orange crystals from Los Lamentos, Chihuahua, Mexico.
Yellow wulfenite with bipyramids from Mežica region, Mount Peca, Slovenia.
Large wulfenite crystals from the Glove mine, near Amado, Arizona.
Type-locality wulfenite from Bad Bleiberg, Carinthia, first described in 1845.
Wulfenite from the Ojuela mine, Mapimí, Durango, Mexico.

kinds.d: Lead chromate mineral specimen: saffron-red to orange prismatic crystals, usually thumbnail to miniature.

x.d: Exceptional crocoite from the Dundas district, Tasmania; the Adelaide mine is called probably the prime source in the world.

v.n: Dundas Extended, Red Lead, West Comet, Platt mines

x.dt: long red prisms · miniature to cabinet

x.d: Type-locality crocoite from Beresovsk, near Yekaterinburg, found in 1766; chromium was discovered in it in 1797.
Crocoite from the Heazlewood, Whyte River and Magnet mines, Tasmania.
Crocoite from Goyabeira, near Congonhas do Campo, Minas Gerais.
Crocoite from Happy Jack, Comet Vale and other places in Western Australia.

kinds.d: Calcium tungstate mineral specimen: glassy dipyramidal crystals that fluoresce bright blue under shortwave UV.

x.d: Scheelite crystals from Pingwu, Sichuan, and the Luoyang area, China.
Large scheelite crystals from the Tae wha mine, Chungju, South Korea.
Scheelite from Cínovec (Zinnwald), Czech Republic, where druses are almost unique.
Scheelite from the Caldbeck Fells, Cumbria.
Type-locality scheelite from Bispberg, Dalarna, Sweden, first described in 1751.
Czochralski-grown scheelite used as a diamond imitation.

kinds.d: Iron tungstate mineral specimen: black bladed crystals, iron end-member of the wolframite series.

x.d: Type-locality ferberite from Sierra de Almagrera, Almería, Spain, named in 1863.
Ferberite from Panasqueira, Portugal.
Well-crystallised ferberite from the Boulder County tungsten district, Colorado.
Large ferberite crystals from Kirwa, Kigezi, Uganda.
Ferberite from Gejui, Hunan, China.

kinds.d: Manganese tungstate mineral specimen: brown to red-black bladed crystals, manganese end-member of wolframite.

x.d: Superb large hübnerite crystals from the Huallapón mine, Pasto Bueno, Ancash, Peru.
x.dt: large blades with quartz and rhodochrosite

x.d: Hübnerite from the Adams mine near Silverton, Colorado.
Hübnerite from the Sweet Home mine, Alma, Colorado.
Type-locality hübnerite from the Erie and Enterprise veins, Nye County, Nevada, named in 1865.
Hübnerite from the Duoluoshan mine, Huaiji, Guangdong.

kinds.d: Hydrous calcium aluminium sulfate mineral specimen: colourless to yellow acicular crystals, notably from N'Chwaning.

x.d: Ettringite crystals from the N'Chwaning mine in the Kalahari manganese fields, South Africa.
Type-locality ettringite from the Ettringer Bellerberg volcano near Mayen, Germany, described in 1874.
Ettringite from the Hatrurim Formation, Israel.
